question: Which type of lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed in clinical practice?

options.A: Bronchial Carcinoid Tumor
options.B: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
options.C: Small Cell Lung Cancer
options.D: Primary Pleural Mesothelioma

explanation: You've got this! Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer accounts for about 85% of all lung cancer cases, making it much more common than the small cell type.

question: Why is checking electrolyte levels like potassium and magnesium vital before giving antiarrhythmics?

options.A: Vitamins and minerals completely cancel out the side effects of antiarrhythmics
options.B: Electrolytes determine how fast the kidneys filter the drug out of the body
options.C: Low minerals cause the intravenous tubing to clog up during administration
options.D: Abnormal electrolyte levels can make the heart more prone to dangerous rhythms

explanation: Electrolyte imbalances directly affect cardiac cell stability and can trigger or worsen arrhythmias despite medication. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h8)

question: Why does severe information asymmetry complicate consumer choice in healthcare?

options.A: Insurance companies forbid patients from choosing doctors
options.B: Patients cannot easily judge the quality or necessity of recommended treatments
options.C: Medical prices change every single hour of the day
options.D: Hospitals refuse to let patients read their own paper charts

explanation: Without specialized knowledge, consumers struggle to evaluate whether a proposed medical service is truly necessary or fairly priced. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary goal of intra-natal care?

options.A: Achieving a safe delivery for mother and baby
options.B: Ensuring the mother sleeps through delivery
options.C: Speeding up the duration of the first stage
options.D: Preventing the need for any pain relief

explanation: The main focus of intra-natal care is to safeguard the health and well-being of both the mother and the newborn throughout labor and birth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T50#GNS214_U1_T50_h1)

question: A nursing instructor wants students to practice taking a health history and showing empathy to an upset patient. Which simulator type is best suited for this?

options.A: A high-fidelity computerized mannequin with chest rise
options.B: A standardized patient who is a trained human actor
options.C: A low-fidelity static arm for practicing venipuncture
options.D: A mid-fidelity mannequin with pre-recorded breath sounds

explanation: Standardized patients are real people trained to act out health conditions and emotional responses, making them ideal for communication practice. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T8#GNS212_U4_T8_h2)

question: At what age do infants in Nigeria routinely receive the yellow fever vaccine?

options.A: At nine months of age
options.B: At eighteen months of age
options.C: At six weeks of age
options.D: At birth before discharge

explanation: Spot on! The immunisation schedule gives the yellow fever shot right at nine months, paired with the measles vaccine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h7)

question: A nursing mother refuses to take her sick child to the clinic because the nearest facility is across a flooded river with no bridge. What primary factor is affecting her health behaviour?

options.A: A lack of personal intelligence
options.B: Stubborn defiance against modern medicine
options.C: An allergic reaction to clinic drugs
options.D: Structural and environmental barriers

explanation: This isn't about her willingness—it's a physical hurdle! Bad roads, long distances, and missing bridges are structural and environmental challenges. You're learning to look at the bigger picture in public health.

question: What is the main purpose of an improvement plan on a hospital ward?

options.A: To reduce the salary budget of the nursing unit
options.B: To turn clinical problems into better patient outcomes
options.C: To punish staff who make medication errors
options.D: To increase the total number of hospital beds

explanation: You've got this! An improvement plan is all about fixing everyday ward challenges step-by-step so that our patients get healthier and safer care.

question: Why do nurses need to explain that emergency contraceptives are not abortifacients?

options.A: To show that they can also cure sexually transmitted infections
options.B: To prove that the drugs are 100 percent effective every time
options.C: To encourage patients to use them instead of regular condoms
options.D: To clear up cultural and moral misconceptions about how the drugs work

explanation: A lot of people mix up emergency pills with abortion pills. As a nurse, clarifying how it actually works helps calm unnecessary fears and clears up social myths. Brilliant work!

question: What kind of muscle weakness or paralysis is typical in polio?

options.A: Flaccid paralysis
options.B: Decerebrate paralysis
options.C: Rigid paralysis
options.D: Spastic paralysis

explanation: Spot on! When lower motor neurons are destroyed, the muscles lose their tone and become limp and floppy—this is known as flaccid paralysis.

question: Which of these is NOT typically a long-term risk of untreated chronic oligomenorrhoea?

options.A: Endometrial cancer
options.B: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
options.C: Iron-deficiency anaemia
options.D: Infertility due to anovulation

explanation: You've got this! Iron-deficiency anaemia happens when someone bleeds *too much* (like menorrhagia). Oligomenorrhoea means infrequent bleeding, so anaemia isn't the primary worry here.

question: A patient suffers a severe spinal cord injury at the level of C2. What major complication do you anticipate?

options.A: Paralysis of the lower legs while retaining full upper body movement
options.B: Inability to move the facial muscles while breathing remains normal
options.C: Loss of sensation only in the hands and lower arms
options.D: Inability to breathe independently due to loss of phrenic nerve function

explanation: Since the phrenic nerve depends on C3 to C5 to function, an injury higher up at C2 cuts off the brain's breathing signals to the diaphragm. Patient safety first! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T26#GNS211_U3_T26_h4)

question: Why do healthcare workers use a team approach (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, etc.) in cancer care?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing involvement in patient education.
options.B: It reduces hospital costs by avoiding diagnostic imaging tests.
options.C: It combines various specialties to ensure accurate diagnosis and comprehensive treatment planning.
options.D: It allows a single doctor to make all clinical decisions without consulting others.

explanation: Cancer care is complex! Working together ensures that every single physical, emotional, and medical need of the patient is met.

question: Why might a nurse choose a non-directive counselling approach for a patient struggling to change their long-term diet?

options.A: It completely removes the nurse from having to guide the session
options.B: It forces the patient to follow doctor orders without asking any questions
options.C: It is the only method allowed for patients in an emergency room trauma bay
options.D: It helps the patient build their own internal motivation and problem-solving skills

explanation: Non-directive counselling empowers clients to find solutions that fit their lives, creating deeper and more lasting personal commitment. [learn more](GNS227_U7_T002#GNS227_U7_T002_h6)

question: What causes the uterine lining to shed at the start of a new menstrual cycle?

options.A: A sharp drop in estrogen and progesterone
options.B: A sudden spike in body temperature
options.C: Implantation of a fertilized egg
options.D: The direct action of FSH

explanation: That is correct! When pregnancy doesn't happen, hormone levels drop, telling the body it's time to shed the lining during menstruation.

question: A Nigerian dietitian is counseling a patient with high blood pressure who has a modest income. What is the most practical advice?

options.A: Recommend affordable local foods and suggest low-salt preparation methods
options.B: Tell the patient to rely entirely on hospital meal deliveries
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating all local carbohydrates completely
options.D: Prescribe expensive imported supplements available only online

explanation: Spot on! Good counseling must fit the patient's pocket. It's always best to recommend healthy, accessible local foods prepared with less salt.

question: Why should nursing leaders join daily safety huddles during a culture change?

options.A: It prevents doctors from questioning the clinical decisions made by nurses
options.B: It proves to staff that leadership values safety and is committed to the change
options.C: It ensures that nurses finish their morning documentation much faster
options.D: It eliminates the need for any further written incident reporting

explanation: Exactly! When leaders 'walk the talk' and show up for frontline safety routines, it builds real trust with the nursing team.

question: Which part of wearing Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is most risky for accidentally contaminating yourself?

options.A: Donning (putting on) the clean gear
options.B: Storing unused aprons
options.C: Doffing (removing) the contaminated gear
options.D: Walking through the hallway

explanation: Correct! Taking off dirty gear takes the most care because you might accidentally touch germs on the outside. Always follow the steps carefully!

question: Why do nurses divide adolescence into different stages?

options.A: It removes the need to talk directly to the patient
options.B: It proves that teenagers will always rebel against authority
options.C: It helps identify normal milestones versus clinical problems
options.D: It stops physical growth from happening too quickly

explanation: Spot on! Breaking adolescence down into stages helps you anticipate what changes are normal and catch any health or developmental delays early.

question: Which condition features flashbacks, avoiding reminders, and being constantly on edge long after a disaster?

options.A: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
options.B: Normal developmental grief
options.C: Acute bronchitis
options.D: Generalized physical fatigue

explanation: Spot on! PTSD is a long-lasting condition where individuals struggle with intrusive memories, avoidance, and a constant 'fight-or-flight' feeling after trauma. [learn more](GNS314_U6_T3#GNS314_U6_T3_h6)

question: Why do qualitative researchers love open-ended questions?

options.A: They make it easy to enter numbers directly into a computer
options.B: They prevent participants from talking about sensitive topics
options.C: They encourage participants to share detailed personal stories
options.D: They guarantee that every interview takes exactly five minutes

explanation: You got it! Open-ended questions give people the freedom to talk in their own words, giving you rich, colourful stories instead of a simple 'yes' or 'no'.

question: When giving eye drops, where is the safest spot to place the liquid?

options.A: Directly onto the center of the cornea
options.B: Into the lower conjunctival sac
options.C: Onto the upper eyelid surface
options.D: Into the inner corner tear duct

explanation: Dropping the medicine into the lower pocket keeps the delicate cornea safe from scratches while letting the drop spread evenly across the eye.

question: What standard p-value do nursing researchers usually look for to prove statistical significance?
explanation: 0.05 is the gold standard in research! It tells us there's a 5% or lower chance our results happened purely by random luck.

question: What is the happy result of successfully narrowing down your nursing research topic?

options.A: The complete elimination of all hospital illnesses
options.B: A specific, manageable question that can be investigated thoroughly
options.C: A massive textbook that covers every disease in medicine
options.D: An automatic guarantee of winning a research award

explanation: When you narrow your focus, you end up with a sharp, clear question that you can actually research, answer, and feel proud of!

question: How many generations should a basic genetic pedigree chart ideally cover?

options.A: At least three generations
options.B: Five to seven generations
options.C: Only the immediate parents
options.D: Just the patient and their children

explanation: Mapping three generations helps reveal patterns of inheritance that might skip a generation or appear across multiple family members. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h2)

question: How can we best describe public health surveillance?

options.A: A method for punishing clinics that lose patient files
options.B: A financial audit of private clinic expenditures
options.C: An ongoing system of collecting and analyzing health data
options.D: A one-time yearly census of hospital bed capacity

explanation: Think of surveillance as a continuous watch, not just a one-off check. We keep gathering and reviewing health data day in and day out to stay ahead of sickness!

question: How does a secondary immune response compare to a primary immune response?

options.A: It produces only short-lived antibodies that cannot destroy viruses.
options.B: It relies entirely on innate barriers rather than white blood cells.
options.C: It causes severe clinical illness because the pathogen is stronger.
options.D: It is faster and produces a much larger amount of antibodies.

explanation: Because of memory cells, the secondary response acts fast and floods your system with antibodies to stop infections early.

question: What is the main idea behind family-centred care when nursing an infant?

options.A: Allowing the nurse to make all home care choices
options.B: Treating the infant as part of a family unit
options.C: Focusing solely on the medical needs of the baby
options.D: Isolating the infant from other family members

explanation: Spot on! Family-centred care treats the baby and the family as one team, making sure you work closely with the loved ones who know the child best.

question: When a low-income Nigerian family faces a sudden medical bill, what is their most common financial backup plan?

options.A: Government health insurance
options.B: Commercial bank loans
options.C: Employer welfare funds
options.D: Extended family networks

explanation: Spot on! Because formal health insurance isn't widespread yet, families usually pull resources together to support sick relatives. You've got this!

question: A patient insists that their mother, who passed away years ago, is coming to visit today. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Argue firmly that the mother is dead to teach them reality
options.B: Scold the family members for not correcting the patient's false memory
options.C: Ignore the comment completely and pretend you did not hear anything
options.D: Acknowledge the feeling behind the statement and gently redirect their attention

explanation: Argueing causes distress. Instead, validate their emotion ('You really miss your mum, don't you?') and gently steer their focus elsewhere.

question: Why does pickling food in an acidic solution stop it from spoiling?

options.A: Acid creates an environment that is too harsh for many pathogens
options.B: Acid removes all the protein content from the food item
options.C: Acid attracts beneficial molds that protect the food surface
options.D: Acid completely freezes the water molecules inside the food

explanation: Most harmful bacteria simply can't handle strong acid. Pickling creates an unfriendly zone where germs can't thrive.

question: Why is avoiding power struggles important when caring for a patient with a personality challenge?

options.A: Arguing escalates tension and rarely changes rigid behavioral patterns
options.B: Patients with personality challenges lack the ability to hear human voices
options.C: Patients always win arguments because nurses are legally not allowed to speak
options.D: Winning a power struggle cures the patient's underlying psychiatric condition instantly

explanation: Engaging in power struggles only increases hostility and frustration, whereas calm, firm boundaries promote better outcomes. [learn more](GNS314_U1_T8#GNS314_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why are typhoid and paratyphoid fevers grouped together as 'enteric fevers'?

options.A: They share very similar clinical presentations and transmission routes
options.B: They can both be cured within twenty-four hours of symptom onset
options.C: They only affect individuals living in cold climates
options.D: They are both caused by viral pathogens affecting the respiratory system

explanation: Spot on! Because they look alike in patients and spread the same way through the gut, we group them together as enteric fevers.

question: What is the main purpose of a health referral system?

options.A: To generate more revenue for large tertiary hospitals
options.B: To prevent patients from ever visiting traditional healers
options.C: To reduce the number of staff needed at rural health posts
options.D: To move patients smoothly between different levels of care

explanation: A referral system connects basic clinics with advanced hospitals to ensure continuous and appropriate patient care. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T16#GNS225_U3_T16_h1)

question: According to Maslow, what must be met before anyone can focus on higher-level needs like self-esteem?

options.A: Peer recognition and leadership roles
options.B: Basic physiological and safety needs
options.C: Advanced professional certifications
options.D: Long-term retirement investment goals

explanation: Think of it like building a house: you need a solid foundation of food, water, and safety before you can worry about chasing big personal goals.

question: What is the standard baseline daily protein recommendation (RDA) for a healthy, less active adult?

options.A: 10 grams per kilogram of body weight
options.B: 5.0 grams per kilogram of body weight
options.C: 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight
options.D: 2.5 grams per kilogram of body weight

explanation: 0.8 grams per kg is the golden baseline set to keep a healthy adult from deficiency and maintain a steady nitrogen balance. Easy to remember for your exams!

question: A nurse leads a support group to help patients with chronic bipolar disorder prevent relapse. What level of prevention is this?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Universal prevention
options.C: Secondary prevention
options.D: Tertiary prevention

explanation: Tertiary prevention involves managing established, chronic conditions to reduce disability and prevent worsening or relapse. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h2)

question: Why do healthcare teams hold professional meetings?

options.A: Coordination and clinical updates among staff
options.B: Evaluating individual nurses on daily bedside tasks
options.C: Replacing all written forms of hospital communication
options.D: Providing a space for extended social interactions

explanation: Meetings bring everyone together to align patient care and share important updates. You'll see this often on the ward!

question: A family is overwhelmed with funeral plans and hospital paperwork right after a death. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Tell them to figure it out since the patient is already gone
options.B: Advise them to ignore all paperwork for at least a month
options.C: Guide them step-by-step and connect them with social work
options.D: Take over their personal bank accounts to pay expenses

explanation: You got it! Offering practical guidance and linking them to social services helps lift the heavy load when they are emotionally exhausted.

question: Why do nurses collect data during quality improvement projects on the ward?

options.A: To prove a brand-new medical theory through controlled trials
options.B: To fulfill mandatory paperwork requirements for the government
options.C: To track the results of small, continuous changes in clinical workflows
options.D: To punish staff members who fail to meet hospital targets

explanation: You've got this! Quality improvement is simply about checking if our daily workflow changes are actually making patient care safer and better.

question: What is the main purpose of a long white cane for mobility?

options.A: To detect ground-level obstacles and uneven surfaces ahead
options.B: To measure the exact distance between walls in a room
options.C: To provide a sturdy walking frame for lower body weakness
options.D: To signal healthcare workers to administer eye medications

explanation: Think of the white cane as an extra helper that sweeps the floor ahead, warning the user about curbs, steps, and obstacles in their path.

question: What is the main job of the large intestine in our daily digestion?

options.A: Producing bile to break down fats
options.B: Absorbing water and compacting waste
options.C: Secreting digestive enzymes for proteins
options.D: Mixing food with stomach acid

explanation: As food waste travels through, the large intestine pulls out the remaining water, turning liquid into solid stool. Spot on!

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge facing DRF exemptions in public hospitals?

options.A: Persistent stockouts caused by lack of reimbursement
options.B: Bureaucratic delays in patient verification
options.C: Exploitation of loopholes by non-indigent individuals
options.D: Excessive government funding that overflows the pharmacy

explanation: If only! Public hospitals rarely have excessive funding; instead, they constantly battle underfunding and delayed subventions.

question: Why does a person's heart beat faster when they have severe anaemia?

options.A: To warm up body tissues chilled by slow blood flow
options.B: To compensate for lower oxygen delivery by pumping blood faster
options.C: To lower high blood pressure from extra red blood cells
options.D: To help the kidneys filter out waste quickly

explanation: Think of it this way: since each drop of blood carries less oxygen, the heart has to pump much faster to make sure vital organs get what they need!

question: What is the safest way for a new mother to clean her perineal area after using the toilet?

options.A: Soaking in soapy bathwater
options.B: Washing from back to front
options.C: Washing from front to back
options.D: Wiping vigorously with dry paper

explanation: Front to back always! This golden rule keeps germs from the anal area away from the vagina and urethra, protecting her from nasty infections.

question: A conscious, alert adult refuses a life-saving treatment based on personal beliefs. Which ethical principle guides you to respect their choice?

options.A: Veracity
options.B: Beneficence
options.C: Justice
options.D: Autonomy

explanation: Well done! Autonomy means a competent patient has the right to decide what happens to their own body, even if we disagree with their choice.

question: Which processing method destroys all microorganisms, including bacterial spores?

options.A: Cleaning
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Disinfection
options.D: Sanitization

explanation: Sterilization is the only process that completely eliminates every form of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which lab test does a nurse watch closely when checking for a worsening skin infection?

options.A: Total red blood cell count
options.B: Serum potassium level
options.C: White blood cell count
options.D: Fasting blood glucose level

explanation: You got it! White blood cells are our immune system soldiers, so high numbers tell us the body is fighting an infection.

question: Why do health guidelines look closely at the *type* of fat we eat, rather than just total grams?

options.A: The body cannot digest saturated fats at all
options.B: Unsaturated fats provide zero energy
options.C: Different fats have very different effects on heart health
options.D: Total fat intake has no effect on body weight

explanation: Not all fats are enemies! While trans fats clog arteries, healthy fats like olive oil protect your heart. It's all about quality over quantity.

question: Why is psychological safety important for nursing staff?

options.A: It prevents patients from ever experiencing any clinical complications
options.B: It guarantees that nurses will receive a salary increase every year
options.C: It allows nurses to report near misses and errors without fear of unfair punishment
options.D: It eliminates the need for doctors to supervise nursing procedures

explanation: When nurses feel safe from unfair punishment, they freely report near misses. This helps the whole team spot hazards and keep patients safe.

question: Where are primary immune cells like lymphocytes born and trained?

options.A: Kidneys and pancreas
options.B: Spleen and lymph nodes
options.C: Bone marrow and thymus
options.D: Liver and gallbladder

explanation: Think of the bone marrow and thymus as the ultimate training camp and academy where vital immune cells are produced and prepped for duty.

question: What does 'unity of command' mean during a disaster response?

options.A: Private businesses take full financial control of public hospitals
options.B: Every individual volunteer acts independently based on personal judgment
options.C: International donors make all final medical decisions on the ground
options.D: Every participating unit reports to a clear, centralized leadership structure

explanation: Unity of command just means everyone answers to one clear leader, which keeps things organized and stops confusion.

question: What is the main purpose of evaluating a public information campaign after a disaster drill?

options.A: To see if the messaging reached the audience and changed behavior
options.B: To increase advertising fees for local television stations
options.C: To punish individuals who failed to follow instructions
options.D: To replace all existing nursing personnel in the facility

explanation: You got it! Evaluating helps health planners see what worked well and what needs fixing for the future.

question: Why must a nurse understand microbial behavior during routine clinical care?

options.A: To eliminate all bacteria permanently from the human body
options.B: To disrupt the infection cycle and protect patients
options.C: To diagnose complex viral mutations without a lab
options.D: To accurately predict drug manufacturing costs

explanation: Knowing how microbes live and spread helps nurses take the right safety steps to stop germs from reaching vulnerable patients. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of client rights in a healthcare setting?

options.A: To ensure that doctors have absolute authority over treatment choices
options.B: To reduce the financial operating costs of running a public hospital
options.C: To give the nursing staff total control over daily ward routines
options.D: To protect the personal dignity and autonomy of the patient

explanation: Client rights exist primarily to safeguard the patient's individual worth and decision-making power while receiving medical care. [learn more](GST321_U10_T5#GST321_U10_T5_h1)

question: What is a major physiological function of the hypodermis?

options.A: Insulating the body against heat loss
options.B: Detecting fine touch and deep pain sensations
options.C: Producing new epidermal skin cells
options.D: Secreting sweat to cool the skin surface

explanation: The layer of fat in the hypodermis acts as thermal insulation, helping to prevent excessive body heat loss to the environment. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h4)

question: A nurse notices that teenage patients look nervous and hesitant when entering the consultation room. What immediate action should the nurse take?

options.A: Refuse to examine the patient until an older family member arrives
options.B: Scold the teenager for being afraid of a routine medical checkup
options.C: Use a warm tone and a welcoming posture to help put the teen at ease
options.D: Insist that a security guard stays inside the room during the interview

explanation: A welcoming attitude and friendly demeanor help break down anxiety and build trust with young clients. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T16#GNS312_U3_T16_h6)

question: What does interoperability mean in the context of health information systems?

options.A: All nurses use the exact same brand of computer tablet
options.B: Patients can print their own physical charts at home
options.C: Different software systems can communicate and exchange data smoothly
options.D: Hospital billing software automatically calculates staff salaries

explanation: Interoperability allows separate technology platforms to share information without manual re-entry. [learn more](GNS113_U2_T4#GNS113_U2_T4_h5)

question: What happens to dissolved oxygen in a body of water when raw sewage creates a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)?

options.A: Oxygen levels drop significantly, suffocating aquatic life
options.B: Oxygen levels remain completely unchanged year-round
options.C: Oxygen turns directly into toxic chlorine gas bubbles
options.D: Oxygen levels rise rapidly, causing plants to grow too fast

explanation: A high BOD means tiny organisms are gobbling up huge amounts of oxygen to break down the waste. This leaves very little oxygen behind for fish and other aquatic creatures to breathe.

question: What is the primary psychiatric condition that antipsychotic medications were originally developed to treat?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Schizophrenia
options.C: Essential hypertension
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Schizophrenia is the main condition these drugs were designed for. They help patients manage reality-distorting symptoms so they can function better.

question: Sudden, heavy weight gain in the second half of pregnancy usually points to what?

options.A: Rapid increase in maternal muscle mass
options.B: Normal development of twin fetuses
options.C: Fluid retention or gestational hypertension
options.D: Excellent absorption of dietary protein

explanation: Spot on! If the scale jumps suddenly along with swelling, it's a red flag for water retention or high blood pressure issues.

question: A nurse researcher assigns hospital wards to receive a new handwashing training program by drawing lots. What experimental element is this?

options.A: Randomization
options.B: Manipulation
options.C: Data saturation
options.D: Blinding

explanation: Drawing lots means choice is left entirely to chance—that is classic randomization in action!

question: Which of these is a quiet sign that a nurse might be showing bias against a PAC patient?

options.A: Providing written educational pamphlets on nutrition
options.B: Unnecessarily delaying care or withholding proper pain relief
options.C: Checking vital signs every fifteen minutes as ordered
options.D: Offering a clean hospital gown and warm blanket

explanation: Sometimes bias shows up as poor treatment—like making a patient wait too long or skipping proper pain meds because of personal judgment.

question: During a pelvic exam, what physical sign would you expect in a patient with Type II FGM?

options.A: A completely sealed vaginal opening with a tiny pinhole
options.B: An intact hymen with no external scars
options.C: Extensive scar tissue and absence of the labia minora
options.D: Enlarged, hypertrophied Bartholin glands

explanation: Well done! The removal of both the clitoris and labia minora leaves clear signs of scar tissue and missing external structures.

question: A patient asks why they got an autoimmune disease while their sibling living in the same house did not. What best explains this?

options.A: Viral infections only affect the oldest sibling in a family
options.B: Differences in genetic susceptibility and individual environmental triggers
options.C: Autoimmune diseases are entirely contagious between household members
options.D: The sibling must have a stronger immune system due to diet

explanation: Even in the same house, no two people have the exact same genes or identical life exposures, which changes everyone's unique disease risk.

question: Which anatomical plane cuts the body into upper and lower sections?

options.A: Sagittal plane
options.B: Midsagittal plane
options.C: Transverse plane
options.D: Frontal plane

explanation: The transverse plane runs horizontally, separating the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) parts. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T2#GNS111_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the main goal of setting up a national health insurance program?

options.A: To replace all doctors with automated medical software
options.B: To achieve nationwide access to healthcare for all citizens
options.C: To restrict healthcare services to high-income earners
options.D: To make public hospitals entirely self-funding

explanation: Well done! National schemes are designed to give every citizen, especially vulnerable groups, fair and easy access to essential medical services.

question: What problem do instructional materials help reduce by giving students a concrete picture of a concept?

options.A: Verbalism
options.B: Dehydration
options.C: Hypertension
options.D: Somnolence

explanation: Verbalism happens when students use or hear words without truly understanding what they mean, which teaching aids prevent by showing the actual object or process. [learn more](GST321_U8_T4#GST321_U8_T4_h2)

question: Which part of the teenage brain is still maturing and plays a big role in impulse control and risk-taking?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Occipital lobe
options.C: Prefrontal cortex
options.D: Medulla oblongata

explanation: Correct! The prefrontal cortex develops slowly into early adulthood, which explains why teenagers sometimes struggle with weighing long-term consequences.

question: What is the minimum recommended fasting time before a fasting blood sugar test?

options.A: 24 hours
options.B: 4 hours
options.C: 8 hours
options.D: 2 hours

explanation: A minimum of 8 hours without caloric intake is required to ensure the digestive system is at rest and baseline glucose can be measured. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T12#GNS221_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why do researchers often recruit more people than their minimum calculated sample size?

options.A: To increase the chance of getting statistically insignificant results
options.B: To account for participants who drop out or withdraw during the study
options.C: To satisfy hospital administrators who love large group numbers
options.D: To make the data entry process longer for student assistants

explanation: Exactly! People travel, fall ill, or change their minds. Adding a buffer upfront saves your project if participants drop out.

question: What is the primary reason nurses must master drug dosage calculations?

options.A: To reduce the workload of the hospital pharmacy
options.B: To speed up the hospital discharge process
options.C: To prevent medication errors and keep patients safe
options.D: To replace the need for physician order sheets

explanation: Accurate calculations ensure the patient receives the exact therapeutic amount, avoiding underdosing or dangerous toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T6#GNS125_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the main job of the thalamus in the brain?

options.A: Coordinating balance and smooth muscle movement
options.B: Relaying and sorting sensory signals to the cortex
options.C: Producing cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles
options.D: Regulating core body temperature and hunger

explanation: Think of the thalamus as the brain's main switchboard, sorting incoming messages and sending them where they need to go.

question: Why must hospitals report certain dangerous infectious diseases to public health agencies?

options.A: To punish doctors who fail to cure their patients quickly enough
options.B: To collect cash rewards offered for rare disease discoveries
options.C: To allow government officials to audit the hospital financial accounts
options.D: To help track and control disease outbreaks in the wider community

explanation: You nailed it! Reporting helps public health authorities spot epidemics early and protect the whole community before it spreads.

question: You need to interview a recovering surgical patient on the ward. Where is the best spot to sit down with them?

options.A: At the main hospital cafeteria during lunch hour
options.B: In a busy hallway right outside the nurses' station
options.C: In a private, quiet room away from routine ward noise
options.D: Inside a crowded emergency department waiting area

explanation: Perfect! Privacy and quiet protect the patient's confidentiality and help them speak openly without feeling exposed.

question: What is the main role of multimodal sensory association areas?

options.A: To store permanent language dictionaries in the brainstem
options.B: To combine inputs from multiple senses into a single experience
options.C: To send initial motor commands directly to skeletal muscles
options.D: To generate raw electrical impulses in the sensory organs

explanation: Multimodal areas act like a mixing desk, taking separate clues from what you see, touch, smell, and hear and blending them into one complete picture of your environment.

question: What term describes the gradual age-related decline of immune system function in elderly adults?

options.A: Immunosenescence
options.B: Immunoglobulin deficiency
options.C: Hypersensitivity reaction
options.D: Autoimmune suppression

explanation: Immunosenescence refers to the natural weakening of the immune system that happens as people grow older. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h6)

question: Which position should an unconscious, non-trauma patient be placed in during transit to prevent aspiration?

options.A: High Fowler's position
options.B: Flat supine position
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Lateral recovery position

explanation: Turning the patient on their side allows fluids to drain safely out of the mouth instead of blocking the airway. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T9#GNS315_U3_T9_h4)

question: What is the main reason labs use differential growth media?

options.A: To completely kill off all unwanted bacteria in a clinical sample
options.B: To preserve the live bacterial sample in the refrigerator for many months
options.C: To increase the total physical size of individual bacterial cells for easy viewing
options.D: To tell different bacteria apart by showing color changes from their chemical reactions

explanation: Well done! Differential media use color changes right on the Petri dish so lab techs can easily spot which bacteria is which.

question: What does 'ring-fencing' mean when managing DRF finances?

options.A: Selling medications only to patients with valid health insurance
options.B: Building a physical fence around the hospital pharmacy store
options.C: Protecting DRF funds so they are only used to buy drugs
options.D: Insuring all drug shipments against theft and fire damage

explanation: Ring-fencing is like putting a protective bubble around the drug money so nobody can borrow it for other hospital bills, keeping the revolving cycle alive!

question: What is the best nursing action when you spot a potential drug interaction on a patient's chart?

options.A: Administer the medications at the exact same time to save nursing time
options.B: Consult the prescriber or pharmacist to discuss a safer alternative or dosage adjustment
options.C: Stop all of the patient's home medications permanently without telling anyone
options.D: Wait until the patient develops physical symptoms before taking action

explanation: Always put patient safety first! As a nurse, you are a key safety barrier—collaborate with your pharmacist or doctor to sort out any red flags before giving the drugs.

question: What is the medical term for seeing double, which happens when the nerves controlling eye movement are messed up?

options.A: Mydriasis
options.B: Ptosis
options.C: Diplopia
options.D: Strabismus

explanation: Diplopia is just the clinical word for double vision. It occurs when the tiny muscles around the eyes aren't working together smoothly.

question: Who is the brilliant thinker behind the System of Profound Knowledge?

options.A: W. Edwards Deming
options.B: Abraham Maslow
options.C: Florence Nightingale
options.D: Jean Watson

explanation: W. Edwards Deming created this popular management framework to help leaders understand and improve organizational systems. You'll see this come up a lot in nursing management!

question: What is the primary medical term for a low salt diet?

options.A: Potassium-depleted diet
options.B: Fluid-restricted diet
options.C: Sodium-restricted diet
options.D: Protein-restricted diet

explanation: A low salt diet is formally called a sodium-restricted diet because it specifically limits sodium intake. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T007#GNS227_U6_T007_h1)

question: What is the main benefit of Omega-3 fatty acids for mental health?

options.A: Clearing harmful toxins directly from the stomach lining
options.B: Supporting neuronal membrane health and reducing depression
options.C: Preventing sudden spikes in blood sugar levels
options.D: Acting as a direct sedative to induce deep sleep

explanation: Omega-3s act like good food for brain cells, helping brain membranes stay healthy and supporting a stable mood.

question: Which of these statements about informed consent in qualitative interviews is FALSE?

options.A: It ensures participants know what the study is about
options.B: It protects the voluntary nature of participation
options.C: It only matters before the interview starts and is then forgotten
options.D: It is a continuous process that can be withdrawn at any time

explanation: You got it! Consent isn't just a paper signed at the beginning—a patient can change their mind and step out of the study at any point.

question: How do learning disabilities differ from global developmental delays?

options.A: Learning disabilities impact every single area of daily physical and mental functioning
options.B: Global delays only appear during adulthood while learning disabilities appear in infancy
options.C: Learning disabilities affect specific academic areas while overall intelligence remains intact
options.D: Global delays are caused exclusively by environmental factors rather than brain function

explanation: Specific learning challenges target isolated skills like reading or math, unlike global delays that affect all areas of development. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h1)

question: What is the main job of luteinizing hormone (LH) in the male body?

options.A: To stimulate testosterone production
options.B: To help mature sperm in the epididymis
options.C: To relax the muscles of the urethra
options.D: To produce the fluid in seminal vesicles

explanation: LH travels through the bloodstream and targets the Leydig cells in the testes, giving them the green light to make testosterone.

question: Why do many patients with chronic kidney disease end up developing anemia?

options.A: The spleen removes healthy blood cells prematurely
options.B: The body destroys red blood cells too quickly
options.C: Dietary iron is no longer absorbed in the gut
options.D: Damaged kidneys fail to produce enough erythropoietin

explanation: You're learning fast! Since sick kidneys can't make enough EPO, the bone marrow doesn't get the signal to build new red blood cells, leading to anemia.

question: A nurse believes a new wound dressing heals ulcers faster. What represents the alternative hypothesis?

options.A: Ulcer healing speed is entirely random and cannot be studied
options.B: Both dressings perform with the exact same level of success
options.C: The new dressing has zero impact on how fast ulcers heal
options.D: The new dressing heals ulcers faster than the standard dressing

explanation: You got it! The alternative hypothesis is simply what the researcher expects to happen—in this case, that the new dressing works better.

question: Which surprising non-food item can also pack a hidden load of sodium for patients?

options.A: Effervescent medications and dissolvable antacids
options.B: Plastic IV catheters used for hydration
options.C: Standard cotton hospital gowns and bedding
options.D: Topical skin moisturizers and lotions

explanation: You nailed it! Medicines that fizz and dissolve in water often use sodium compounds to get that reaction, adding sneaky sodium to the day.

question: What is a crucial check a nurse must do before giving any mucous membrane medication?

options.A: Instruct the patient to hold their breath for two minutes
options.B: Apply a thick layer of petroleum jelly over the site
options.C: Crush the medication to speed up local absorption
options.D: Inspect the target membrane for irritation or lesions

explanation: Always take a quick look first! Checking the tissue ensures there are no open sores or heavy irritation that could make absorption painful or unsafe for the patient.

question: What is the primary purpose of the cold chain system?

options.A: Transporting medical personnel safely to remote rural outposts
options.B: Preventing theft of expensive pharmaceutical supplies in storage
options.C: Freezing needles and syringes to sterilize them before use
options.D: Keeping vaccines at the correct temperature to preserve their potency

explanation: Biological vaccines are sensitive to heat and require strict temperature controls to remain effective against diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h3)

question: What happens in the uterus right after a patient takes mifepristone?

options.A: Muscles relax completely to prevent any early spotting
options.B: The myometrium immediately begins violent cramping
options.C: The uterine lining breaks down and the cervix softens
options.D: Blood vessels expand to increase oxygen delivery to the fetus

explanation: Spot on! By blocking progesterone, mifepristone gets the uterus ready and softens the cervix before the second drug is even taken.

question: How does strong teamwork help protect nurses from burnout?

options.A: Nurses are excused from direct bedside patient care duties
options.B: Hospital administrations eliminate all night shifts and weekend work
options.C: The heavy mental load of complex patient management is shared
options.D: Doctors take over all charting and documentation responsibilities

explanation: You got it! When the team shares responsibilities and talks things through, the heavy stress of patient care feels much lighter.

question: What hormone must be released by a developing embryo to keep the corpus luteum alive?

options.A: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
options.B: Testosterone
options.C: Human chorionic gonadotropin
options.D: Luteinizing hormone

explanation: Embryonic human chorionic gonadotropin signals the corpus luteum not to degenerate, ensuring continued hormone support for the pregnancy. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T3#GNS216_U2_T3_h6)

question: When should a sharps disposal container be safely sealed and replaced?

options.A: Only when it is completely overflowing at the top
options.B: At the very end of every calendar month
options.C: When it reaches the three-quarters full mark
options.D: As soon as the first single syringe is dropped inside

explanation: Stopping at three-quarters full prevents needles from poking out of the opening and endangering staff who handle the waste. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T67#GNS214_U1_T67_h5)

question: What is an essential component of any upward referral from a nurse?

options.A: Cash payment for the specialist consultation at the tertiary gate
options.B: A clear clinical summary letter detailing history and current medications
options.C: A personal guarantee that the client will be admitted as an inpatient
options.D: Official approval from the local government chairman

explanation: Always send a proper handover note! A clear clinical summary helps the specialist know what you've tried and what the patient needs next.

question: What do endocrine glands release straight into the bloodstream?

options.A: Hormones
options.B: Mucus
options.C: Saliva
options.D: Enzymes

explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands don't use ducts; they release hormones straight into our blood to act as chemical messengers all over the body.

question: What usually happens on the ward when a nurse struggles with poor time management?

options.A: Decreased physical fatigue among nursing staff
options.B: Higher patient satisfaction scores across the unit
options.C: Increased risk of missed care and medication errors
options.D: More time available for professional development

explanation: True! When things get too rushed and we lose control of our time, important tasks or meds can easily slip through the cracks. Take a breath—learning how to pace yourself helps prevent this!

question: What typically happens during the clinical latency stage of an untreated HIV infection?

options.A: The immune system completely clears the virus from the body.
options.B: The patient immediately develops terminal opportunistic infections.
options.C: The virus replicates slowly while the patient may have few symptoms.
options.D: Red blood cells multiply rapidly to compensate for tissue damage.

explanation: Well done! During latency, the virus is still active but multiplies at a low level, and the person might feel completely well for years without treatment.

question: Why do nurses need to be extra careful with the membranous segment of the male urethra during catheter insertion?

options.A: It is the narrowest and least stretchable part, making it prone to injury.
options.B: It expands dramatically to hold large volumes of urine before release.
options.C: It is filled with sensitive nerve endings that cause severe pain.
options.D: It sits right outside the body where infection enters easily.

explanation: Good clinical awareness! Because this section is narrow and less flexible, gentle handling and correct technique are key when passing a catheter.

question: What is another name for the body's specific defense system?

options.A: Adaptive immune system
options.B: Innate barrier response
options.C: Non-specific defense network
options.D: Mechanical protection layer

explanation: We call them specific defences the adaptive immune system because they adapt and target exact germs over time. You've got this!

question: What is considered the first and most fundamental function of nursing management?

options.A: Controlling
options.B: Planning
options.C: Directing
options.D: Staffing

explanation: Planning comes first because it sets the direction and goals before any other management function can take place. [learn more](GST321_U1_T6#GST321_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of community mobilisation?

options.A: Enforcing strict national health laws in rural villages
options.B: Replacing traditional healers with modern medical doctors
options.C: Collecting financial taxes for local health clinics
options.D: Empowering community members to solve local problems together

explanation: Community mobilisation focuses on bringing people together so they can take charge of their own health issues and find local solutions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h1)

question: What happens when a germ changes its target binding site?

options.A: The drug can no longer attach to the microbe effectively
options.B: The drug becomes toxic to human liver cells
options.C: The microbe begins producing extra doses of the antibiotic
options.D: The human immune system destroys the bacterial cell wall

explanation: Drugs need to lock onto a specific part of a pathogen to work. If the microbe alters that shape, the drug just slides right past!

question: In the emergency ABCDE assessment framework, what does the letter 'D' stand for?

options.A: Drainage
options.B: Defibrillation
options.C: Diagnosis
options.D: Disability

explanation: That's right! 'D' stands for disability, which is a quick check of the patient's level of consciousness and brain function.

question: In the chain of infection, what do we call the cozy home base where a germ lives, grows, and multiplies?

options.A: Susceptible host
options.B: Portal of entry
options.C: Reservoir
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: Think of a reservoir as a germ's favorite hangout spot—like a human body, an animal, or a damp surface where it can multiply!

question: Which of these is NOT a common hurdle when setting up reproductive health networks?

options.A: Logistical constraints like poor roads and stock-outs
options.B: Inter-agency rivalry and bureaucratic silos
options.C: Deep-rooted cultural stigma and moral judgment
options.D: Universal access to unlimited financial resources for all clinics

explanation: You got it! Clinics usually struggle with chronic shortages of cash, so having unlimited funds is definitely not a reality or a barrier!

question: What is the primary purpose of doing maternal death reviews in a hospital?

options.A: To reduce the number of patients seeking antenatal care
options.B: To satisfy international funding agencies without changing practice
options.C: To find a junior nurse to blame for an unavoidable accident
options.D: To discover systemic failures and prevent similar future tragedies

explanation: Maternal death reviews are never about witch-hunts. They help the team figure out what went wrong in the system so we can protect mothers next time. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T2#GNS312_U5_T2_h7)

question: A patient comes in with a severe infection and a high fever. What should the nurse expect to happen to their metabolic rate?

options.A: Metabolic rate remains completely unchanged
options.B: Metabolic rate drops to zero
options.C: Metabolic rate increases significantly
options.D: Metabolic rate fluctuates only during sleep

explanation: Fever acts like stepping on the gas pedal for your cells! Chemical reactions speed up, which is why febrile patients burn through energy so fast.

question: What is the most accurate way to measure energy use in a critical care patient?

options.A: Indirect calorimetry
options.B: Skinfold caliper tests
options.C: Standard food diaries
options.D: Body mass index charts

explanation: Indirect calorimetry measures the gases a patient breathes out to figure out their exact calorie needs. It's the gold standard in the ICU!

question: What is a common nutrition mistake people make when switching to packaged gluten-free foods?

options.A: Consuming too much natural protein from fresh fruits and vegetables
options.B: Eating too many processed substitutes lacking fiber and B vitamins
options.C: Developing an immediate intolerance to all dairy products
options.D: Suffering from severe protein toxicity due to meat overconsumption

explanation: It's easy to rely on packaged gluten-free snacks, but many lack the fiber and vitamins found in whole or fortified foods.

question: Why must you always place a weighing scale on a hard, flat surface before taking a reading?

options.A: To prevent the patient from feeling dizzy while standing
options.B: To protect the delicate internal electronic circuits from moisture
options.C: To make it easier for the nurse to read the digital screen
options.D: To ensure the weight distribution is even and the reading is accurate

explanation: Well done! Soft or uneven surfaces (like thick tiles with gaps or carpets) absorb pressure and mess up the scale's accuracy.

question: Why can damage to the pons mess up normal sleep patterns?

options.A: It monitors blood oxygen levels specifically while sleeping.
options.B: It houses neural circuits that regulate REM sleep and muscle relaxation.
options.C: It directly generates conscious awareness during the night.
options.D: It controls the production of melatonin in the pineal gland.

explanation: Pontine structures play a big role in dreaming (REM sleep) and making sure our muscles stay relaxed so we don't act out our dreams.

question: What is the medical name for the condition where a baby's foot is twisted inward and downward?

options.A: Congenital talipes equinovarus
options.B: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
options.C: Spina bifida occulta
options.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta

explanation: That's just the fancy clinical term for clubfoot! You'll hear 'talipes equinovarus' a lot in your pediatric postings.

question: Why is it best to use both quantitative and qualitative methods during your community assessment?

options.A: It is required by law to spend extra ministry funding
options.B: It prevents nurses from having to speak to villagers directly
options.C: It combines measurable statistics with deep human context
options.D: It ensures that no written reports need to be created

explanation: Numbers give you the stats (how many people are sick), but talking to people gives you the story (why they are sick and what stops them from getting help). You need both!

question: A patient keeps visiting the clinic with headaches and stomach upset, but all lab tests come out normal. What should you suspect?

options.A: Unresolved psychological stress manifesting as physical symptoms
options.B: A severe vitamin deficiency requiring immediate surgery
options.C: An accidental poisoning caused by community water supply
options.D: A rare tropical infection that laboratory tests cannot detect

explanation: When the lab results are completely clear but the pain is real, the body is often speaking the language of unexpressed stress (somatization).

question: Which of these is an example of a viral causative agent?

options.A: Staphylococcus bacteria
options.B: Malaria protozoa
options.C: Ringworm fungus
options.D: Influenza virus

explanation: Great job! Viruses like the flu need a living host cell to multiply, unlike bacteria or fungi.

question: Which pathway carries nerve signals toward the central nervous system?

options.A: Sympathetic division
options.B: Efferent division
options.C: Afferent division
options.D: Autonomic division

explanation: A-fferent arrives at the brain (think 'A' for arrival). You'll master these terms in no time! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T2#GNS211_U3_T2_h4)

question: How was the role of a nurse different in early asylum days compared to modern nursing?

options.A: Nurses focused exclusively on intensive individual psychotherapy
options.B: Nurses were primarily responsible for prescribing antipsychotic medications
options.C: Nurses spent most of their time running community outreach clinics
options.D: Nurses functioned mainly as guards focused on physical containment and order

explanation: Correct! Back then, security came before healing, so nurses spent a lot of their time managing locked doors and enforcing physical control instead of therapeutic care.

question: A patient runs out of insulin two weeks after a storm destroys nearby pharmacies. What type of disaster impact is this?

options.A: Technological impact
options.B: Acute biological impact
options.C: Indirect impact
options.D: Direct impact

explanation: When health problems pop up later because medical supplies got cut off, we call that an indirect impact. Every question you try makes you a better nurse!

question: What is the primary goal of rehabilitation services for special children?

options.A: To keep the child confined to a hospital bed
options.B: To eliminate the need for any assistive technology
options.C: To completely cure all genetic and congenital disorders
options.D: To maximize independence and improve quality of life

explanation: Rehabilitation focuses on helping children function at their highest possible level despite chronic limitations. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T6#GNS225_U5_T6_h5)

question: Which simple tool do nurses use right in the field to quickly check if a child is suffering from malnutrition?

options.A: A pulse oximeter
options.B: A standard blood pressure cuff
options.C: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape
options.D: A peak flow meter

explanation: The colorful MUAC tape is a nurse's best friend in community outreaches and disaster zones for spotting malnutrition in seconds.

question: Which of these is a major challenge to quality assurance in many Nigerian healthcare settings?

options.A: Shortages of nursing personnel and equipment
options.B: Excessive funding for nursing research programs
options.C: Too many nurses working in rural health centers
options.D: An overabundance of advanced medical technology

explanation: Unfortunately, staff shortages and a lack of basic tools are very real hurdles we face when trying to maintain high care standards in many of our hospitals.

question: A patient is transferred from a rural clinic to a city teaching hospital. How does an interoperable EHR system help the nurse?

options.A: By stopping all medications until a new doctor sees the patient
options.B: By providing instant access to past lab results and medical history
options.C: By forcing the nurse to wait for mailed paper files
options.D: By automatically discharging the patient when they arrive

explanation: Interoperable EHRs let receiving facilities pull up past medical records immediately, which avoids delays in ongoing care. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T1#GNS113_U3_T1_h2)

question: How does an autoclave sterilize infectious waste?

options.A: By freezing the waste to extremely low temperatures
options.B: By soaking the waste in strong liquid bleach
options.C: By using high-pressure steam to kill pathogens
options.D: By crushing the waste into tiny metal cubes

explanation: Autoclaves use heat, moisture, and high pressure to destroy infectious microorganisms effectively before disposal. [learn more](GST114_U6_T12#GST114_U6_T12_h7)

question: Why is coaching the patient to take deep breaths so important during an unsedated sigmoidoscopy?

options.A: It helps relax their belly and pelvic muscles, making it easier to pass the scope.
options.B: It removes the need for lubrication.
options.C: It keeps their blood pressure artificially high.
options.D: It keeps them from swallowing air into their lungs.

explanation: Spot on! When cramps hit, patients naturally tense up. Deep breathing helps them relax those muscles so the procedure goes smoother.

question: If a needle absolutely must be recapped in an emergency, what is the safest way to do it?

options.A: Holding the cap in your mouth while positioning the syringe
options.B: Using both hands to snap the cap back on firmly
options.C: The one-handed scoop technique
options.D: Asking an untrained assistant to hold the cap for you

explanation: Always use the one-handed scoop method! It keeps your free hand safely out of the way, preventing accidental needle pricks.

question: What makes a Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) so great for a busy rural health clinic?

options.A: It gives quick results from a finger-prick blood sample without complex equipment
options.B: It permanently prevents future mosquito bites from causing infection
options.C: It is the only test capable of identifying dead parasites after treatment
options.D: It tells the nurse the exact number of parasites circulating in the blood

explanation: Spot on! RDTs are fast, portable, and a lifesaver in clinics where there are no fancy lab machines or steady electricity.

question: Which of the following is NOT a normal nursing duty when caring for an adolescent with a pubertal development issue?

options.A: Referring the family to a pediatric endocrinologist for evaluation
options.B: Providing gentle psychological reassurance to the anxious patient
options.C: Monitoring growth charts and physical milestones over time
options.D: Surgically removing the pituitary gland without a doctor's order

explanation: Correct! Nurses never perform unauthorized surgery. Your role focuses on assessment, emotional support, patient education, and coordinating care.

question: Which of the following is NOT a safe finding and requires immediate reporting during a postpartum home visit?

options.A: Slight breast tenderness as milk production begins
options.B: Foul-smelling vaginal discharge and a low-grade fever
options.C: Normal postpartum fatigue after a night of interrupted sleep
options.D: Mild lochia rubra that gradually decreases over two weeks

explanation: Foul-smelling discharge and fever point toward a uterine infection (endometritis), which requires prompt medical evaluation and antibiotics. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T13#GNS324_U3_T13_h5)

question: How does hospice philosophy view the dying process?

options.A: As an unpredictable event requiring intensive surgery
options.B: As a natural part of the human life cycle
options.C: As a condition that can always be reversed with therapy
options.D: As a medical failure that must be fought at all costs

explanation: Hospice care embraces dying as a normal stage of life rather than viewing it purely as a medical failure. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h2)

question: What is a major financial benefit of healthcare PPPs for the government?

options.A: Stopping all government spending on public health infrastructure
options.B: Shifting capital investment and financial risk to the private sector
options.C: Eliminating the need to collect taxes from citizens for health
options.D: Guaranteeing that hospitals will never operate at a financial loss

explanation: Private partners bring in big money upfront for building and equipment, which takes a huge financial weight off the government's shoulders.

question: What is the biggest risk of failing to track post-meeting action items?

options.A: Staff members will forget how to write clinical reports
options.B: The hospital will immediately fail its financial audit
options.C: Future meetings will become legally invalid
options.D: Decisions are forgotten and important tasks are left undone

explanation: Without tracking and follow-up, even the best plans discussed in meetings fade away into nothing.

question: A researcher decides to pick every 5th patient from the clinic register. Which sampling method is this?

options.A: Snowball sampling
options.B: Quota sampling
options.C: Convenience sampling
options.D: Systematic sampling

explanation: You nailed it! Going down a list at regular intervals (like every 5th or 10th person) is called systematic sampling.

question: Which of these is NOT a sign that a uterine perforation might have happened?

options.A: Sudden relief from all abdominal cramping
options.B: Tenderness across the lower abdomen
options.C: Severe and worsening lower abdominal pain
options.D: Signs of internal bleeding and low blood pressure

explanation: A perforated uterus causes worsening pain and tenderness—not sudden relief! Always watch out for sharp abdominal pain after instrumentation.

question: What must a nurse always do before starting any care in a patient's home?

options.A: Publishing the care plan in a national newspaper
options.B: Receiving written approval from local community leaders
options.C: Consulting the hospital board of directors
options.D: Obtaining proper informed consent from the patient

explanation: Always! Respecting our patients means getting their clear okay before doing any checks or procedures.

question: What is a primary clinical responsibility of a psychiatric nurse in a CBR program?

options.A: Ordering all medical supplies directly from international factories
options.B: Managing the financial budget of the national ministry of health
options.C: Constructing physical buildings for local primary health centers
options.D: Monitoring medication compliance and watching for signs of relapse

explanation: Nurses regularly check if clients are taking their drugs correctly and observe for early behavioral changes that indicate the illness might be returning. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T3#GNS314_U5_T3_h3)

question: A nurse sees a public social media post from someone asking for medical advice about an open wound. What is the safest and most professional action?

options.A: Write a detailed treatment plan in the public comments section
options.B: Refrain from giving specific personal diagnoses and suggest they visit a clinic
options.C: Ignore the post and share pictures of the ward to cheer them up
options.D: Share the hospital's internal secure password with the commenter

explanation: Giving casual medical advice online creates legal liability and fails to provide safe, formal clinical assessment. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T9#GNS113_U1_T9_h7)

question: You need to scan patient bands and check medications right at the bedside using a portable device. Which computer type do you grab?

options.A: An analog monitor for blood pressure waves
options.B: A supercomputer used for genomic research
options.C: A microcomputer like a tablet or mobile workstation
options.D: A mainframe computer in the hospital basement

explanation: Brilliant! Tablets and mobile carts are handy microcomputers designed to move with you right to the patient's bedside.

question: Which condition is linked directly to hypothalamic damage that messes up fluid balance?

options.A: Diabetes insipidus
options.B: Diabetes mellitus
options.C: Chronic insomnia
options.D: Hemiballismus

explanation: Well done! When the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary is damaged, anti-diuretic hormone drops, causing the massive water loss seen in diabetes insipidus.

question: What is the maximum amount of medication you should give in a single intradermal injection site?

options.A: 1.0 to 2.0 mL
options.B: 0.1 to 0.5 mL
options.D: 3.0 to 5.0 mL

explanation: Correct! The dermis is a tight little space. If you push more than 0.5 mL in there, it will either damage the tissue or leak right out.

question: What is a major advantage of field research over laboratory research?

options.A: It gives the researcher total control over the weather
options.B: It requires no permission from ethics committees
options.C: It eliminates all possible errors in data entry
options.D: It reflects real-world conditions and natural behaviors

explanation: Brilliant! Field research happens out in natural settings, making the findings much easier to relate to everyday human life. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h5)

question: How is an epidemic different from an endemic disease?

options.A: An endemic illness only appears once every ten years in a community.
options.B: An epidemic represents a sudden spike in cases above the normal expected baseline.
options.C: An endemic condition spreads much faster than any known epidemic.
options.D: An epidemic only affects people living in cold weather climates.

explanation: Great thinking! While an endemic disease is steady and expected, an epidemic breaks that baseline with an unusual, sudden surge of new cases.

question: When does a patient maintain a stable body weight?

options.A: Energy intake equals energy expenditure
options.B: Energy intake drops to zero for a day
options.C: Energy intake exceeds energy expenditure
options.D: Energy expenditure is higher than energy intake

explanation: Weight remains stable when the total calories consumed match the total calories burned by the body. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T006#GNS227_U4_T006_h1)

question: What is the very first thing an infection control team does when investigating a possible outbreak?

options.A: Fire the nursing supervisor in charge of the affected ward
options.B: Immediately shut down the entire hospital and send all patients home
options.C: Verify the diagnoses and clearly define what counts as a case
options.D: Hold a press conference to warn the public about the danger

explanation: Spot on! Before hunting for the source, you first need to be sure real infections are happening and set clear rules for what you are counting.

question: What is the core golden rule behind standard precautions in nursing?

options.A: Treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
options.B: Sterilizing disposable plastic syringes for reuse
options.C: Isolating only patients with confirmed laboratory diagnoses
options.D: Using gloves only when blood is visibly dripping

explanation: Standard precautions mean we treat every patient's blood and body fluids as if they could carry an infection. Safety first, always!

question: What is the main purpose of giving Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT)?

options.A: To replace lost fluids and electrolytes
options.B: To provide daily nutritional caloric requirements
options.C: To stop the underlying infection causing diarrhea
options.D: To reduce the frequency of bowel movements

explanation: ORT doesn't stop the infection or the stooling right away. Its primary job is to put back the water and essential mineral salts that are washed out during vomiting and diarrhea.

question: What is a frequent, painful problem caused by excessive pushing during bowel movements in pregnancy?

options.A: Gestational diabetes
options.B: Placental abruption
options.C: Preeclampsia
options.D: Hemorrhoids

explanation: You got it! Straining puts heavy pressure on the pelvic veins, which often leads to swollen, painful hemorrhoids (piles).

question: Besides physical safety, what else helps create a healing ward environment?

options.A: Playing loud music to keep patients awake during the day
options.B: Keeping the lights at maximum brightness twenty-four hours a day
options.C: Allowing visitors to stay without any time limits
options.D: Reducing noise and addressing patient grievances promptly

explanation: You've got this! Healing isn't just physical—lowering stress by keeping noise down and listening to patient complaints makes a huge difference.

question: After fats are broken down in the small intestine, where do they go first?

options.A: Blood capillaries directly
options.B: The large intestine wall
options.C: Lymphatic lacteals
options.D: The gastric mucosa

explanation: Unlike sugars and amino acids that jump straight into blood capillaries, digested fats take a special detour through tiny lymphatic vessels called lacteals first!

question: Why does the inner lining of the small intestine contain millions of villi and microvilli?

options.A: To secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes straight into the mouth
options.B: To maximize the surface area available for absorbing nutrients
options.C: To produce strong muscular contractions for moving food forward
options.D: To neutralize the acidic chyme coming directly from the stomach

explanation: The villi and microvilli create a massive surface area that allows digested food particles to pass efficiently into the blood and lymph vessels. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T8#GNS213_U3_T8_h1)

question: A teenager comes in with severe monthly belly pain but no menstrual bleeding. Which condition is the most likely cause?

options.A: Bacterial vaginosis
options.B: Vaginal agenesis
options.C: Atrophic vaginitis
options.D: Transverse vaginal septum

explanation: Well done! A transverse septum acts like a wall blocking menstrual blood from getting out, leading to trapped blood, swollen tissues, and intense monthly pain even though her uterus is working fine.

question: Why do we need 'multisectoral collaboration' to effectively control NCDs?

options.A: Hospitals do not have enough medical equipment to treat infectious diseases
options.B: Government policies can only be implemented by doctors and surgeons
options.C: Nurses are not qualified to talk to patients about diet and exercise
options.D: Risk factors like poor diet, tobacco use, and physical inactivity require action from many societal sectors

explanation: You nailed it! Fighting NCDs goes beyond the hospital; it involves agriculture, education, finance, and urban planning working together as a team.

question: What is considered the absolute best (gold standard) way to confirm a nasogastric tube is in the right spot?

options.A: Measuring the length of tubing left outside the nose
options.B: Listening for air sounds over the belly with a stethoscope
options.C: Checking for water drops inside the clear plastic tube
options.D: Abdominal X-ray

explanation: An X-ray gives us clear visual proof that the tip is sitting comfortably in the stomach before we start any feeding.

question: How is a pandemic different from an epidemic?

options.A: It disappears completely after a period of three weeks
options.B: It spreads across multiple countries and continents worldwide
options.C: It only affects livestock rather than human populations
options.D: It maintains a low, steady baseline in a single village

explanation: While an epidemic can be massive, a pandemic goes global, crossing international borders to affect people all over the world.

question: What is the primary purpose of the teach-back method in nursing communication?

options.A: Checking if the patient truly understands their care instructions
options.B: Testing the patient's ability to read medical textbooks
options.C: Giving the nurse a break from talking during long shifts
options.D: Proving that the nurse explained the procedure correctly

explanation: The teach-back method asks patients to repeat instructions in their own words, revealing any confusion before they leave the clinic. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T12#GNS124_U5_T12_h4)

question: Which body system is in charge of releasing the hormones that trigger puberty?

options.A: The urinary system
options.B: The endocrine system
options.C: The respiratory system
options.D: The lymphatic system

explanation: Spot on! The endocrine system is made up of glands that send hormones straight into your bloodstream to guide important body changes like puberty.

question: How do azole antifungal medications mostly work against fungi?

options.A: By blocking bacterial folic acid synthesis
options.B: By stimulating human white blood cell production
options.C: By dissolving the outer viral protein capsule
options.D: By altering fungal cell membrane permeability

explanation: Antifungals poke holes in the fungal cell membrane (by attacking things like ergosterol). This makes all the important cell contents leak out!

question: What actually opens the ion channels on a touch receptor when you press on the skin?

options.A: Physical stretching of the cell membrane
options.B: Hormonal changes in the blood
options.C: A drop in core body temperature
options.D: Electrical shocks from the brain

explanation: Think of it like a tiny trapdoor: when you press on the skin, the physical stretch pulls the cell membrane open so ions can flow through!

question: As a psychiatric nurse, how should you view a patient's mental health symptoms when you first meet them?

options.A: As deliberate choices made to upset family members
options.B: As proof that the patient lacks all willpower
options.C: As an attempt by the psyche to protect itself
options.D: As permanent brain damage that cannot heal

explanation: Every symptom has a backstory. When we view symptoms as the mind's clumsy way of shielding itself from pain, it becomes much easier to care for our patients without judgment.

question: Which historic international conference officially launched the modern concept of Primary Health Care (PHC) back in 1978?

options.A: The Abuja Health Summit
options.B: The Geneva Health Accord
options.C: The London Nursing Conference
options.D: The Alma-Ata Declaration

explanation: Spot on! The 1978 conference in Alma-Ata set the global standard for making basic health services accessible to everyone right in their communities.

question: Which of the following is NOT a known complication of intrapleural drug therapy?
